title: p0145
universal_lens: The gradient of reinforcement formalizes the spatial-temporal decay of reward signals. It unifies learning curves by mapping proximal actions to asymptotic value limits, establishing a foundational kernel for deriving secondary behavioral phenomena and optimizing state-transition probabilities across complex decision manifolds.
gsi_mapping: GSI models the reinforcement gradient as a Bayesian posterior decay function over event horizons. Conformal inference bounds quantify the uncertainty of proximal action-value estimates, ensuring robust predictive calibration when extrapolating performance metrics from localized historical data to broader temporal scales.
gse_mapping: In GSE, the gradient dictates situational state transitions. The rate of rise (F) maps to immediate tactical execution velocity, while the limit of rise (m) defines strategic equilibrium. This operator governs dynamic agent adaptation within constrained environmental topologies.

primitives.name: Gradient Decay Extent Operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: How far does this gradient extend from the point of reinforcement before falling approximately to zero?
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: L: Effective horizon (dimensionless trials or seconds), \tau: Temporal/spatial lag from reinforcement, V: Value function (utility units), \epsilon: Negligible threshold (utility units)
primitives.assumptions: Continuous differentiable decay of value V with respect to lag \tau; existence of a finite effective horizon.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularities occur in non-Markovian environments where delayed rewards induce long-tailed distributions, causing L to diverge.

layer2.mapping: Maps directly to the look-ahead horizon in Monte Carlo tree search and credit assignment windows in deep reinforcement learning.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical measurement of trial intervals yielding statistically significant performance improvements.

primitives.name: Asymptotic Learning Kernel
primitives.verbatim_quote: What parameters of the curve of learning are affected by the gradient of reinforcement—the rate of rise (F), or the limit of rise (m), or both?
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: P(t): Performance at time t (success probability), m: Asymptotic performance limit (dimensionless), F: Rate of acquisition (inverse time), t: Training duration (time)
primitives.assumptions: Exponential saturation dynamics; constant environmental feedback structure during the learning phase.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks down under catastrophic interference or non-stationary reward landscapes where m dynamically shifts.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to GSI Elo-rating convergence rates and GSE tactical execution efficiency matrices.
layer2.telemetry: Regression analysis of success rates over sequential trials to extract F and m.

primitives.name: Axiomatic Primacy Evaluator
primitives.verbatim_quote: Is the relationship a primary principle or is it a secondary one; i.e., can it be derived from other and more basic principles?
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: \mathcal{O}: Ontological status (categorical), \Psi: Observed behavioral law, \Phi: Underlying potential field, \nabla: Derivation operator
primitives.assumptions: Behavioral laws form a hierarchical lattice; reductionist derivability is well-defined.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Emergent systems exhibiting irreducible complexity where macro-behavior cannot be reduced to micro-potentials.

layer2.mapping: Determines whether a GSI feature is a fundamental primitive or a composite derivative of underlying biomechanical constraints.
layer2.telemetry: Model parsimony metrics (e.g., AIC/BIC) comparing direct fits vs. derived latent variable models.

We derive three sovereign primitives to formalize these concepts for quantitative modeling. First, the Gradient Decay Extent Operator quantifies the spatial-temporal reach of a reward signal, defining the boundary condition where influence approaches zero. This establishes the effective horizon for credit assignment in sequential decision-making. An actor anticipates that an opponent's behavior is governed by specific rate (F) and limit (m) parameters derived from past reinforcements. By estimating the decay extent of the adversary's reward signals, a strategic agent can exploit blind spots—areas where the opponent's gradient falls to zero—thereby inducing suboptimal state transitions and maximizing expected utility.
